title: Why Statistics?
text:
In a world overflowing with data, statistics is your key to making sense of it all. It’s not just about numbers—it’s about uncovering the stories they tell and turning uncertainty into clarity. Statistics empowers you to make informed decisions, spot hidden trends, and transform data into actionable insights. Whether you’re navigating business challenges, analyzing research, or simply curious about the world, mastering statistics equips you with the tools to decode complexity and drive meaningful results. Dive into statistics and unlock the true potential of data!
Here are a few compelling reasons why learning statistics is essential:

title: Why Statistics?
text:
Data-Driven Decision Making

Informed Decisions: Statistics enables you to make decisions based on data rather than intuition or assumptions. Whether in business, science, or daily life, understanding trends, risks and probabilities helps you make more accurate and confident decisions.
Risk Assessment: In the fields like finance, insurance, or medicine, statistics helps assess risks, allowing for more informed risk management.

title: Why Statistics?
text:
Essential in Many Fields

Business and Economics: Statistical methods are used to analyse market trends, customer behaviour, and financial performance. Statistical models help forecast sales, optimize pricing strategies and improve operations.
Medicine and Healthcare: It is crucial in medical research for evaluating the effectiveness of treatments, understanding disease spread, and analyzing clinical trials.
Social Sciences: In areas like psychology, sociology and political science, statistics helps to analyze survey data, test hypothesis ,and understand social phenomena.
Natural Sciences: From biology to physics, statistics is crucial for analyzing experimental results, testing scientific theories, and making sense of large data sets.
Technology and Data Science: In data science, machine learning and AI, statistics forms the foundation for algorithms, models, and data analysis.

title: Why Statistics?
text:
Understand the world

Analyze Information Critically: With rise of big data we are constantly bombarded with statistics in the news, politics , and advertising. Learning statistics help you assess the accuracy of information, spot misleading claims and avoid manipulation.
Make Sense of Uncertainty: Many real world phenomena involve uncertainty, and statistics is the science of dealing with this uncertainty.

title: Why Statistics?
text:
Improved Research Skills

Designing Studies: Statistics teaches you how to properly design experiments and surveys, ensuring that data collected is meaningful and unbiased. This is essential in conducting valid research.
Hypothesis Testing: It allows researchers to determine whether their results are statistically significant, meaning they are not just due to chance. This is critical component in scientific discovery.
Analyzing Data: Statistics equip you with tools to analyze, interpret, and extract insights from data, turning raw data into meaningful conclusions.

title: Why Statistics?
text:
Logical and Analytical Thinking
Statistics develops critical thinking, logic and problem solving skills, which are valuable beyond numerical data analysis. It fosters analylitical reasoning that is applicable in any field.

title: Why Statistics?
text:
Career Opportunities

In-Demand Skill: In today’s data driven world , statistical skills are highly sought after. Many job roles including data scientists, analysts, market researchers require statistical knowledge.
Interdisciplinary: Learning statistics opens doors to diverse career paths since it is used in fields like economics, engineering, healthcare, psychology, marketing and even sports.

title: Why Statistics?
text:
Personal and Professional Development

Better Understanding of Research: With statistics, you can critically evaluate research papers, articles and studies.
Solve Real World Problems: Statistics helps in solving complex real world problems by offering structured approaches to analyze and interpret data.

title: Why Statistics?
section: Foundation for Data Science and Machine Learning
text:
Foundation for Data Science and Machine Learning

Core to Data Science: Statistics is the backbone of data science, helping with everything from data collection, cleaning and exploration to building predictive models.
Machine Learning Models: Many machine learning algorithms such linear regression, decision tress, and clustering have roots in statistical techniques. Understanding statistics enables a better grasp of how these models work and how to improve them.

title: What is Statistics?
text: The following definitions fit well on the subject of Statistics. They are taken from different authors:

title: What is Statistics?
text:
Major Branches of Statistics
There are two major branches of statistics:

Descriptive Statistics: Concerned with organisation, summarization description of data.
Inferential Statistics: Involves using sample data to generalize the population.

title: Types of Data
text: We have three types of data qualitative, quantitative and ranked data. Any statistical analysis is performed on data. The precise form of statistical analysis often depends on the type of data.

title: Types of Data
text:
Qualitative Data
A set of observations where any single observavation is a word, letter or numerical code that represents a category.

title: Types of Data
text:
Ranked Data
A set of observations where any single observation is a number that indicates relative standing.

title: Types of Data
text:
Quantitative Data
A set of observations where a single observation is a number that represents an amount or a count.
Each type of data goes with a level of measurement. A level of measurement specifies the extent to which a number (or word or letter) actually represents some attribute and therefore, has implications for the appropriateness of various arithmetic and statistical procedures.

Nominal Measurement: Words, letters, or numerical codes of qualitative data that reflect differences in kind based on classification.
Ordinal Measurement: Relative standing of ranked data that reflects differences in degree based on order.
Interval/Ration Measurement: Amounts or counts of quantitative data reflect differences in degree based on equal intervals and a true zero.

title: Common Statistical Definitions
text:
Below are some common statistical definitions:

Population: Any complete collection of observations or potential observations
Sample: Any smaller collection of actual observation from the population
Random Sampling: A procedure designed to ensure that each potential observation in the population has an equal chance of being selected in a survey
Random Assignment: A procedure designed to ensure that each person has an equal chance of being assigned to any group in an experiment
Homogeneity: Similarity among individuals within a population
Parameter: A descriptive measure of the characteristics calculated on a population
Sample statistic: A descriptive measure on a sample

title: Understanding Normal Distribution in R
text:
📊 What is the Normal Distribution?
A normal distribution is a bell-shaped, symmetric distribution centered at the mean (μ) and defined by the standard deviation (σ).

Key Properties:

About 68% of values lie within ±1σ of the mean
About 95% within ±2σ
About 99.7% within ±3σ


# Visualizing a standard normal distribution
x <- seq(-4, 4, length = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x)

plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "blue",
     main = "Standard Normal Distribution",
     xlab = "Z-score", ylab = "Density")
abline(v = 0, col = "black")
abline(v = c(-1, 1), col = "gray", lty = 2)
abline(v = c(-2, 2), col = "gray", lty = 2)
abline(v = c(-3, 3), col = "gray", lty = 2)

title: Understanding Normal Distribution in R
text:
🧠 Z-Scores
A Z-score tells us how many standard deviations a value is from the mean:
\[
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
\]

Positive z → above the mean
Negative z → below the mean

title: Understanding Normal Distribution in R
text:
📈 Using pnorm() in R
pnorm() gives the probability to the left of a given value:
pnorm(q, mean = μ, sd = σ, lower.tail = TRUE)

Examples:

1. P(X < 78), where μ = 70, σ = 6

pnorm(78, mean = 70, sd = 6)  # ≈ 0.9082

[1] 0.9087888




2. P(X > 140), where μ = 120, σ = 10

1 - pnorm(140, mean = 120, sd = 10)  # ≈ 0.0228

[1] 0.02275013




3. P(110 < X < 135), μ = 120, σ = 10

pnorm(135, 120, 10) - pnorm(110, 120, 10)  # ≈ 0.7745

[1] 0.7745375

title: Understanding Normal Distribution in R
text:
🔁 Using qnorm() in R
qnorm() gives the cutoff value (X) for a given cumulative probability:
qnorm(p, mean = μ, sd = σ, lower.tail = TRUE)

Examples:

1. What score corresponds to the 90th percentile (μ = 500, σ = 100)?

qnorm(0.9, mean = 500, sd = 100)  # ≈ 628.16

[1] 628.1552




2. What is the cutoff for the fastest 10% of reaction times (μ = 250, σ = 30)?

qnorm(0.10, mean = 250, sd = 30)  # ≈ 211.55

[1] 211.5535

title: Understanding Normal Distribution in R
section: 🧪 Practice Problems with Solutions and Visualizations
text:
🧪 Practice Problems with Solutions and Visualizations

Problem 1: Proportion below a score
A test has μ = 70, σ = 6. What proportion scores below 78?


Show Answer
pnorm(78, 70, 6)  # ≈ 0.9082

# Visualize
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 70, sd = 6), from = 40, to = 100, lwd = 2, col = "blue",
      ylab = "Density", main = "P(X < 78), μ = 70, σ = 6")
polygon(c(40, seq(40, 78, length.out=100), 78),
        c(0, dnorm(seq(40, 78, length.out=100), 70, 6), 0),
        col = "skyblue")




Problem 2: Between two scores
Systolic BP: μ = 120, σ = 10. Find the proportion between 110 and 135.


Show Answer
pnorm(135, 120, 10) - pnorm(110, 120, 10)  # ≈ 0.7745

# Visualize
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 120, sd = 10), from = 80, to = 160, lwd = 2, col = "blue",
      ylab = "Density", main = "P(110 < X < 135), μ = 120, σ = 10")
polygon(c(110, seq(110, 135, length.out=100), 135),
        c(0, dnorm(seq(110, 135, length.out=100), 120, 10), 0),
        col = "skyblue")




Problem 3: Fastest 10% (lowest tail)
Find the score that cuts off the fastest 10% for a test with μ = 250, σ = 30.


Show Answer
qnorm(0.10, 250, 30)  # ≈ 211.55

# Visualize
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 250, sd = 30), from = 150, to = 350, lwd = 2, col = "blue",
      ylab = "Density", main = "Fastest 10% (X < 211.55), μ = 250, σ = 30")
polygon(c(150, seq(150, 211.55, length.out=100), 211.55),
        c(0, dnorm(seq(150, 211.55, length.out=100), 250, 30), 0),
        col = "skyblue")

title: Which regression method for binary outcome?
text:
# Load necessary packages
library(dplyr)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
library(gtsummary)
library(flextable)
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Simulated dataset (350 individuals)

early_sex <- data.frame(
  early_sexual_debut = rbinom(350, 1, 0.3),  # Binary outcome (30% prevalence)
  exposed = rbinom(350, 1, 0.5),  # 50% exposed
  age = sample(18:30, 350, replace = TRUE),  # Age range 18-30
  education = factor(sample(c("None", "Primary", "Secondary", "Higher"), 350, replace = TRUE), labels = c("None", "Primary", "Secondary", "Higher")),
  gender = factor(rbinom(350, 1, 0.4), labels = c("Male", "Female"))
)

title: Which regression method for binary outcome?
text:
1. Logistic Regression: The Default Choice?
Logistic regression is often the first choice for binary outcomes because it models the log odds of an event occurring. It estimates odds ratios (ORs), which tell us how much more or less likely an event is in one group compared to another.

When to use: Logistic regression is ideal when the outcome is rare (<10%).
Why? Odds ratios approximate relative risks well in rare events but become misleading when outcomes are common.

We will explore both univariable and multivariable regression

waldci <- function(x, exponentiate =  TRUE, conf.level = 0.95, ...) {
  dplyr::bind_cols(
    broom::tidy(x, exponentiate = exponentiate, conf.int = FALSE),
    # calculate the confidence intervals, and save them in a tibble
    exp(stats::confint.default(x)) %>%
      tibble::as_tibble() %>%
      rlang::set_names(c("conf.low", "conf.high"))  )
}


univariable.regress <- function(covariates, modeltype="logistic") {
  
  form <- paste("early_sexual_debut", "~",
                paste(covariates, collapse = " + "))
  
  if (modeltype == "logistic"){
    
    model <- early_sex |> 
      select(all_of(vars), early_sexual_debut) %>%
      tbl_uvregression(tidy_fun = waldci,
      method = glm,
      y = early_sexual_debut,
      method.args = list(family = binomial(link = "logit")),
      exponentiate = TRUE,
      pvalue_fun = function(x) style_pvalue(x, digits = 2)) %>% 
      modify_column_hide(stat_n)
    
    
    est <- "**OR**"
  } else if (modeltype == "logbinomial"){
    model <- early_sex |> 
      select(all_of(vars), early_sexual_debut) %>%
      tbl_uvregression(tidy_fun = waldci,
      method = glm,
      y = early_sexual_debut,
      method.args = list(family = binomial(link = "log")),
      exponentiate = TRUE,
      pvalue_fun = function(x) style_pvalue(x, digits = 2)) %>% 
      modify_column_hide(stat_n)
    
    est <- "**PR**"
  } else if (modeltype == "modifiedpoisson"){
    model <- early_sex |> 
      select(all_of(vars), early_sexual_debut) %>%
      tbl_uvregression(tidy_fun = waldci,
      method = glm,
      y = early_sexual_debut,
      method.args = list(family = poisson(link = "log")),
      exponentiate = TRUE,
      pvalue_fun = function(x) style_pvalue(x, digits = 2)) %>% 
      modify_column_hide(stat_n)
    est <- "**PR**"
  }
  
   
  
 model  |> 
  bold_p() %>%
  bold_p(t = 0.05) %>%
  bold_labels() %>% 
  modify_header(label = "**Variable**",
                estimate = est) %>% 
  modify_table_styling(
    columns = c("conf.low", "estimate"),
    rows = reference_row %in% TRUE,
    missing_symbol = "Ref"
  ) |> 
  as_flex_table() %>%
  font(fontname = "Calibri", part = "all") %>%
  autofit() %>%
  padding(padding = 1, part = "all") %>%
  fontsize(size = 10)
  

}



mvariable.regress <- function(covariates, modeltype="logistic") {
  
  form <- paste("early_sexual_debut", "~",
                paste(covariates, collapse = " + "))
  
  if (modeltype == "logistic"){
    model <- glm(as.formula(form),
      data = early_sex, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
    est <- "**adjusted OR**"
  } else if (modeltype == "logbinomial"){
    model <- glm(as.formula(form),
      data = early_sex, family = binomial(link = "log"))
    est <- "**adjusted PR**"
  } else if (modeltype == "modifiedpoisson"){
    model <- glm(as.formula(form),
      data = early_sex, family = poisson(link = "log"))
    est <- "**adjusted PR**"
  }
  
   
  
 model  %>% 
    tbl_regression(tidy_fun = waldci,
    exponentiate = TRUE
  ) %>%
  bold_p() %>%
  bold_p(t = 0.05) %>%
  bold_labels() %>% 
  modify_header(label = "**Variable**",
                estimate = est) %>% 
  modify_table_styling(
    columns = c("conf.low", "estimate"),
    rows = reference_row %in% TRUE,
    missing_symbol = "Ref") 
  

}

univariable.regress("logit")

section: 2. Log-Binomial Regression: Directly Estimating Prevalence Ratios (PRs)
text:
2. Log-Binomial Regression: Directly Estimating Prevalence Ratios (PRs)
The log-binomial model is an alternative when we want to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs) directly. Unlike logistic regression, which estimates odds, log-binomial regression models probability, making the interpretation more intuitive.

When to use: Suitable for cross-sectional studies where the outcome prevalence is not rare.
Limitation: This model sometimes fails to converge, making computation tricky.


Univariable Log Binomial Regression

univariable.regress("logbinomial")

VariableOR195% CI1p-valueexposed1.170.73, 1.860.51age1.020.96, 1.090.46genderMaleRefRefFemale0.860.53, 1.370.52educationNoneRefRefPrimary0.830.43, 1.630.59Secondary0.820.42, 1.620.57Higher0.940.50, 1.790.861OR = Odds Ratio, CI = Confidence Interval




Multivariable Log Binomial Regression

logbinmodel <- mvariable.regress(vars, "logbinomial")

title: Which regression method for binary outcome?
section: 3. Modified Poisson Regression: A Practical Alternative for PRs
text:
3. Modified Poisson Regression: A Practical Alternative for PRs
To address convergence issues with log-binomial regression, modified Poisson regression is commonly used. This approach uses Poisson regression with robust standard errors to estimate PRs correctly.

When to use: When the outcome is common (>10%) and PRs are preferred over ORs.
Advantage: More stable and easier to compute than log-binomial regression.
Standard Poisson regression assumes variance = mean (which often isn’t true)
The sandwich estimator corrects for overdispersion and provides valid confidence intervals for Prevalence Ratios
Without robust SEs, confidence intervals may be too narrow.
With robust SEs (sandwich estimator), we get valid PR estimates.


Univariable Modified Poisson Regression

univariable.regress("modifiedpoisson")

Final Thoughts
Understanding when to use ORs, PRs, or RRs can significantly impact how we interpret study results. While logistic regression remains the standard, recognizing when to use log-binomial or modified Poisson regression ensures we report measures that align with study goals and accurately reflect risk or prevalence.


Conclusion
I conclude with what Louise-Anne McNutt1 had to say:


The use of an adjusted odds ratio to estimate an adjusted relative risk is appropriate for studies of rare outcomes, however, may be misleading when the outcome is common. The overestimation may inappropriately affect clinical decision-making or policy development. Additionally, overestimation of the importance of a risk factor may lead to unintentional errors in the economic analysis of potential intervention programs or treatments. Options exist to obtain unbiased estimates of relative risks in studies of common outcomes. Two methods that have widely available user-friendly software and often are statistically appropriate (e.g., fit the data) include stratified analysis and log-binomial modeling.
